youtube.title: How the Great Salt Lake Lost 22 Feet
youtube.description:
On October 10, 2026, the Great Salt Lake fell to 4,189.4 feet, less than a foot above its all-time low, and Utah's officials say one more dry winter would make a new record in 2027 unavoidable. Forty years ago the same lake was flooding, and the state pumped it into the desert. We follow the water from the 1980s flood to today's exposed lakebed: what drained it, what its dust may mean for the Wasatch Front, and what it would take to refill it.

Real Copernicus Sentinel-2 and NASA MODIS images, USGS lake-level data and our own calculations.
youtube.pinned_comment: Who should give up water first so the Great Salt Lake can recover: the farms, the cities, or no one at all? Where do you stand?

paragraphs.text: This is the Great Salt Lake in June 2017: Antelope Island, and Farmington Bay to its right. Now watch the same shore in October 2026.

On October 10th the lake fell to 4,189.4 feet above sea level, less than a foot above the lowest level ever recorded. Utah's own officials have said that another winter like the last one would make a new record in 2027 unavoidable.

stat.label: above the all-time low, on October 10, 2026

shots.on_screen_text: State officials: a 2027 record 'unavoidable' after another dry winter

paragraphs.text: Forty years ago the problem ran the other way. The lake was flooding, and Utah spent about 60 million dollars pumping it into the desert.

shots.on_screen_text: 1987: pumping the lake into the desert

paragraphs.text: So how does a lake go from flooding to failing in one lifetime? And who pays when its dry bed starts to blow?

shots.subtitle: The Great Salt Lake, from flood to record low

paragraphs.text: The Great Salt Lake has always risen and fallen. It is the shrunken remnant of Lake Bonneville, an Ice Age lake up to 1,000 feet deep that covered about 20,000 square miles, a little less than West Virginia. About 16,000 years ago it cut an outlet at its northern end and poured out in an enormous flood. Its old shorelines are still visible on the mountains above Salt Lake City.

document.highlight: the shrunken remnant of prehistoric Lake Bonneville
document.title: Great Salt Lake, Utah, Water-Resources Investigations Report 99-4189

stat.label: covered by Lake Bonneville, a little less than West Virginia
stat.note: up to 1,000 ft deep, about 30,000 to 16,000 years ago

shots.query: Wasatch mountains Salt Lake City aerial

paragraphs.text: In 1963 it fell to 4,191.35 feet, a record low that stood until 2021. Then wet winters came one after another, and from January 1983 to June 1986 the lake rose more than ten feet, to 4,211.6 feet, the highest level on record. At that size it was more than twice as large as in 1963.

chart.title: Great Salt Lake, feet above sea level

paragraphs.text: The water reached roads, farms and wildlife areas along the shore. Stretches of Interstate 80 had to be raised as much as eight feet. The railroad raised its causeway across the lake, and in the summer of 1983 it lined the embankment with more than 1,400 old railroad cars to break the waves. In 1986 the south end was diluted enough that killifish swam in from Timpie Springs. By one estimate, the flood years did more than 240 million dollars of damage, in 1985 dollars.

stat.label: old railroad cars lined the causeway against the waves, 1983

paragraphs.text: So Utah decided to pump the lake into the desert. A federal study from July 1986 laid out the plan: a pumping station on the lake's far western shore, and canals to carry the water into a desert basin around the Newfoundland Mountains. Pumping began on April 10th, 1987.

document.title: West Desert Pumping Project, Final Environmental Impact Statement, July 1986
document.source: Bureau of Land Management, U.S. Department of the Interior (public domain)

paragraphs.text: In twenty-six months the pumps moved 2.7 million acre-feet of water west. Then the wet years ended, and on June 30th, 1989, the pumps were switched off. The lake has been falling, on and off, ever since.

stat.label: acre-feet pumped into the desert, April 1987 to June 1989

chart.title: Great Salt Lake, lowest level each year

paragraphs.text: The lake has no outlet. Three rivers feed it, the Bear, the Weber and the Jordan, and on average about 2.9 million acre-feet of water reach it each year. It loses water only to evaporation, so its level is a simple sum: what flows in, minus what the sun takes.

shots.on_screen_text: Average inflow: 2.9 million acre-feet a year

shots.query: sun glare over salt lake water

paragraphs.text: Before those rivers reach the lake, farms and cities take their share. A 2017 study in Nature Geoscience estimated that water use since the 1850s has lowered the lake by about 11 feet and cut its area nearly in half. Agriculture accounts for more than 60 percent of that use.

document.text: Decline of the world's saline lakes

stat.label: lower because of water use since the 1850s
stat.note: and an area cut nearly in half

paragraphs.text: Then came the winter of 2025 to 2026. On February 1st, Utah's snowpack hit a record low. Snow supplies about 95 percent of the state's water, and by mid-February, 93 percent of Utah was in drought. It was the same dry winter that sent Lake Powell to its record low.

shots.query: thin snow mountains Utah winter drought

stat.label: of Utah in drought, mid-February 2026
stat.note: snow supplies about 95 percent of the state's water

shots.at: It was the same dry winter

paragraphs.text: Wet years still help. After the winter of 2023, the lake rose almost five feet in six months, and by October 2026 it was back where it started. So which drained it more: the dry winters, or more than 150 years of water use? Tell me where you land.

chart.title: Great Salt Lake, feet above sea level

ask.text: Dry winters or water use: what drained the lake more?

paragraphs.text: From orbit, the lake shows two colors. The Southern Pacific Railroad built a causeway across it from 1956 to 1959, for about 53 million dollars, and split it in two. The rivers flow into the southern part, so the north arm turned far saltier, and salt-loving microbes tint it pink.

shots.photo: NEAR THE UNION PACIFIC RAILROAD CAUSEWAY. THE CAUSEWAY THREATENS THE ECOLOGICAL BALANCE OF THE LAKE - NARA - 544757.jpg

paragraphs.text: Since 1966, the north arm has averaged 317 grams of salt per liter. The south arm averages 142, still about four times as salty as the ocean.

In 1972 a federal photographer documented the causeway for the Environmental Protection Agency. The caption said it threatened the lake's ecological balance. In 1984, during the flood, it was breached near Lakeside, and in 2016 the railroad opened a 180-foot gap so the two arms could mix more freely.

shots.photo: THE UNION PACIFIC RAILROAD'S CAUSEWAY ACROSS THE GREAT SALT LAKE THREATENS THE ECOLOGICAL BALANCE OF THE LAKE - NARA - 544761.jpg
NEAR THE UNION PACIFIC RAILROAD CAUSEWAY. THE CAUSEWAY ENDANGERS THE ECOLOGICAL BALANCE OF THE LAKE - NARA - 544772.jpg

stat.label: the gap opened in the causeway in 2016
stat.note: so the two arms can mix more freely

paragraphs.text: That salty water is also an industry. The lake supplies 35 to 40 percent of the world's brine shrimp eggs, which fish and shrimp farms buy as feed. In 2012 the harvest was worth about 57 million dollars.

stat.label: of the world's brine shrimp eggs come from the lake
stat.source: Great Salt Lake Advisory Council study, 2012

stat.label: brine shrimp harvest from the lake, 2012
stat.source: Great Salt Lake Advisory Council study, 2012

paragraphs.text: Here is the whole lake in September 2000, seen by NASA's Terra satellite, and here it is in October 2026. About 800 square miles of lakebed now lie exposed.

shots.on_screen_text: About 800 sq mi of lakebed exposed

paragraphs.text: That bed holds arsenic and other metals. When the wind lifts it, the dust can blow toward Salt Lake City and the cities of the Wasatch Front. University of Utah researchers found that the dust falls hardest on disadvantaged neighborhoods, and a U.S. Geological Survey study listed arsenic as a contaminant of concern if the dust is swallowed. Atmospheric scientist Kevin Perry has told lawmakers that dust levels have, on occasion, broken national air standards.

Utah's Division of Air Quality reads the record differently. It says the Wasatch Front meets the federal standard for coarse dust, and that a decade of monitoring shows no rise in airborne arsenic as the lake has dropped. The disagreement is about exposure: how much dust people actually breathe, and how often.

There is a precedent in California. Owens Lake, drained by Los Angeles's water diversions, was for years the country's largest source of man-made coarse dust. The city's water department says its dust controls have cost more than 2.5 billion dollars and cover 48.6 square miles. The exposed bed of the Great Salt Lake is more than sixteen times that area. So should Utah pay now to keep water in the lake, or wait for clearer proof of harm?

shots.on_screen_text: Owens Lake dust controls: 48.6 sq mi

stat.label: spent on dust control at Owens Lake, California
stat.note: 48.6 sq mi of controls; dust down 99.4 percent
stat.source: Los Angeles Department of Water and Power

shots.on_screen_text: Great Salt Lake: about 800 sq mi exposed, more than 16 times Owens Lake's controls

ask.text: Pay to refill the lake now, or wait for proof of harm?

paragraphs.text: More than 12 million birds of 339 species use the lake. On one day in July 1991, scientists estimated 600,000 Wilson's phalaropes here, more than a third of the world's population, and up to five million eared grebes gather on the lake, at times more than half of all those in North America. Since 1992 it has been part of the Western Hemisphere Shorebird Reserve Network.

stat.label: birds of 339 species use the lake
stat.note: a third of the world's Wilson's phalaropes stop here

stat.label: Wilson's phalaropes on one day, July 1991
stat.note: more than a third of the world's population

shots.query: flock of birds flying over lake

paragraphs.text: The lake also makes snow. Storms that cross it pick up moisture, and that adds an estimated 5 to 8 percent of Utah's snowfall. If you want to see where the shoreline stands after next spring's runoff, subscribe: we will check it again from orbit.

shots.query: ski resort Utah powder snow aerial

stat.label: of Utah's snowfall comes from the lake

paragraphs.text: Put together, a 2012 study for the state counted about 1.3 billion dollars of yearly output and 7,700 jobs tied to the lake. A 2019 report estimated that losing it could cost Utah 1.7 to 2.2 billion dollars a year and more than 5,000 jobs.

chart.title: Great Salt Lake economy, billion dollars a year
data: Yearly cost if it dries, low (2019)
Yearly cost if it dries, high (2019)

paragraphs.text: In 2024 the state's Great Salt Lake commissioner set a goal: keep the lake between 4,198 and 4,205 feet. It ended the 2025 water year at its third-lowest level in more than 120 years, about seven feet below that range. From October's low, reaching it would take a rise of 8.6 feet.

stat.label: the range Utah set as the lake's goal in 2024

chart.title: Great Salt Lake, lowest level each year
ref: 4,198 ft: the low end of the goal

stat.label: to climb to the low end of the goal
stat.note: 4,198-4,205 ft (2024 strategic plan); 4,189.4 ft on October 10, 2026
stat.source: Great Salt Lake Commissioner; USGS; our calculation

paragraphs.text: The plan's own estimate is steep: about a million extra acre-feet a year in drought years, a third on top of the lake's average inflow, and 471,000 in normal years. A strike team of state and university experts estimated that reaching 4,198 feet by 2055 would take about 800,000 extra acre-feet every year.

stat.label: extra acre-feet a year the lake needs in drought years
stat.note: about a third on top of its average inflow of 2.9 million
stat.source: Great Salt Lake Strategic Plan 2024; USGS; our calculation

chart.title: Extra water the lake needs, acre-feet a year

stat.label: extra acre-feet a year to reach 4,198 ft by 2055

paragraphs.text: The 2026 legislature put close to 100 million dollars toward the lake and made it easier to send it water, including excess water from cities and counties. Critics told KSL that the biggest gap is still how much water cities use. Lawmakers have also rejected a resolution to make 4,198 feet a legal goal. Should Utah set a legal minimum for the lake?

stat.label: close to this much for the lake from Utah's 2026 session
stat.note: plus faster water transfers to the lake

ask.text: Should Utah set a legal minimum for the lake?

paragraphs.text: State officials did not expect a new record this year, and so far the lake has stayed just above it. In mid-August it stood at 4,190.4 feet, on October 10th at 4,189.4, and by November 3rd it had crept back to 4,190.0. One more dry winter, they have said, would make a record in 2027 unavoidable.

So the lake's future depends on two things: the snow that falls this winter, and how much water people let reach it. Who should give up water first: the farms, the cities, or no one at all? Tell me what you think.
